article.title: The One More Room Journal
article.description: Nithin (38, engineering manager) & Divya Prasad's (36, senior data scientist) pandemic outgrowth — a 2.5BHK that became two desks, a villa detour priced like a pressed flower, a buyer who ghosted two links up the chain, and a PLH 4BHK closed with the reversibility thesis: office today, bedroom tomorrow.
article.quote: "The dining table has been two desks for three years. We surrender."

tabs.title: Who they are
tabs.description: Nithin, 38, engineering manager at a SaaS firm (3 days office, Bellandur); Divya, 36, senior data scientist (fully remote since 2021). Two children, 7 and 3. They bought a 2.5BHK in Sobha Dream Acres in 2019 — a correct decision the pandemic quietly outgrew — and the whole search runs on one firm sentence: 'we need two more rooms, and one of them must be an office with a door.'

chatMessages.text: Riya, we're standing in the 'fourth bedroom' of the second PLH unit. Nithin is doing the thing.

The door closes — actual door, solid. North light till about two pm. LAN conduit behind the switchplate, checked. Now the real test. Divya, go to the corridor and be a seven-year-old. …Faint. Genuinely faint, kada. This wall has actual masonry self-respect.

That's the first unit of six to pass the scream test. So let's talk about what passing means: this one is three-point-six-two all-in; with the tenant continuing at forty-five, your net outflow lands at thirty-four percent — inside your own rule. Bedroom three takes a desk with east light — mornings are yours, Divya — and the day one of you stops remote work, it's a bedroom again in an afternoon. That reversibility is the whole 4BHK thesis. The two-loan stress test holds — I ran it while Divya was screaming. I'll draft the offer.

tabs.insightTitle: What I noticed while we were searching
tabs.insightDescription: “Nithin and Divya taught me that the pandemic's most common real-estate aftershock is the family whose home stopped matching its floor plan in 2020 — and the search runs on one firm sentence: two more rooms, one of them an office with a door. The office audit (door, light, LAN, call-acoustics) disqualified two 4BHKs whose fourth 'bedroom' was a corridor with a window — square footage lies, floor plans under-lie, site visits at call-time tell the truth. The villa detour's real value was a written boundary: EMI plus fees at 45%, which ended every future stretch conversation in one line. And the hinge was the ghosting: their buyer disappeared after token because his own chain collapsed upstream — the lesson structural: never let your purchase depend on your sale's buyer's sale. They kept the flat, signed a tenant at forty-five thousand, reworked the loan at higher LTV, and closed a PLH 4BHK at three-point-six. The walkthrough ended in the empty fourth room — one desk chair, everyone barefoot — because the reversibility thesis is the whole 4BHK: an office today, a bedroom again in an afternoon.”

First resales from original owners in a township you already know are the upgrader's sweet spot: seasoned documents, nil GST, a proven community, and sellers who remember being you. checklistItems: Your current home was right when you bought it and the pandemic rewrote its job description.
At least one career in the house is permanently remote, and the dining table has been a desk for years.
You need two more rooms and one must be a genuine office — door, light, acoustics — not an alcove with ambitions.
You're an upgrader: selling or leveraging one flat to buy the next, which makes you both supply and demand in someone's chain.
The school run and the community fabric are fixed points; the floor plan is the variable.
You've toured the villa, done the math, and chosen the airbag over the garden — or you're one reel away from that tour.

roadmapNodes.title: L1: The Two-Desks Breaking Point
roadmapNodes.desc: The 2.5BHK's dining table is now two desks; the second child's cot shares the study wall; 'we need one more room' becomes 'we need two.'

roadmapNodes.title: L2: The Keep-Vs-Sell Fork
roadmapNodes.desc: Sell (down payment power) vs rent out (₹45K/month, but LTV and two-property nerves) — the model with the third prong, keep-and-leverage, circled.

roadmapNodes.title: L3 DETOUR: The Villa Dream
roadmapNodes.desc: PLH villas toured after a Sunday reel — ₹5.42–6.5 Cr; three weeks of 'what if we stretch' before the school-fees-plus-EMI math restores the 4BHK thesis.

roadmapNodes.title: L4: The 4BHK Shortlist
roadmapNodes.desc: PLH large apartments (2,600–2,830 sqft resale) vs Sobha Neopolis 4BHK (new, possession 2027 vs a school year) vs Brigade Cornerstone Utopia's largest units (value).

roadmapNodes.title: L5: The Ghosted Sale
roadmapNodes.desc: Their 2.5BHK buyer ghosts after token (his own upgrade chain collapsed upstream); pivot: rent it out instead, rework the loan at higher LTV.
roadmapNodes.loopText: Chain Failure — Buyer Ghosted After Token, Converted to Keep-and-Leverage

roadmapNodes.title: L6: The Office Audit Sharpens
roadmapNodes.desc: North light, door that closes, LAN conduit, call-acoustics — a ROOM, not a niche; two units fail on 'study = corridor alcove.'
roadmapNodes.loopText: The Office Audit — Door, Light, LAN, and the Scream Test

roadmapNodes.title: L7: The Empty Fourth Room
roadmapNodes.desc: PLH 4BHK (2,700 sqft class) closed ~₹3.6 Cr with tenant continuity on their 2.5BHK; the walkthrough ends in the empty fourth room where both offices finally exist.
